Information since February still fits a “dovish hike” narrative—labor remains strong, growth moderate, inflation near 2%, and the Fed raised the funds rate to 0.75–1.00% while stressing that policy is accommodative, increases will be gradual, and data-dependent, with IOER at 1.00% and ON RRP at 0.75% anchoring short rates. Incorporating SLOOS, however, adds nuance: banks and foreign banks expect tighter standards for CRE and construction/land development, and banks anticipate tighter auto standards with deteriorating asset quality in autos and credit cards; foreign banks also reported weaker business loan demand. Offsetting that, C&I standards are currently unchanged with some banks expecting to ease, and banks anticipate easing for certain residential mortgage categories (e.g., GSE-eligible and jumbo), with little change for prime segments like GSE-eligible mortgages and HELOCs. On net, the SLOOS points to mixed but slightly tighter credit supply in riskier segments and potential consumer-credit headwinds, which reinforces the Committee’s cautious, flexible inflation-targeting stance and makes the hike look even more “dovish” in context.
